40 Which particle is a fundamental particle?
A
electron
B
hadron
C
neutron
D
proton

hints: Look at the four names given - electron, hadron, neutron and proton - and ask which ones are built from quarks.
Remember that any hadron is defined as a quark composite, and that proton and neutron are the two common examples of baryons.
Recall where the electron fits as a lepton with charge $-e$ and no $u$ or $d$ quark content, meaning it cannot be broken into smaller constituents.
walkthrough: Start from the definition: a fundamental particle has no internal structure and is not made of any smaller particles.
Hadrons are composite particles made of quarks held together by the strong interaction, so anything described as a hadron cannot be fundamental.
Check the nucleons: a proton has quark composition $uud$ and a neutron has quark composition $udd$, so both are baryons and therefore hadrons with internal structure.
Check the electron: it is a lepton, not a quark composite, and in the Standard Model leptons and quarks are the fundamental building blocks.
Only the electron has no smaller constituents, so it is the fundamental particle. This is option A

A.explanation: The electron is a lepton with no quark structure and no known smaller parts, so it is fundamental in the Standard Model.

B.explanation: A hadron is a family of particles made of quarks, so by definition it is composite and not fundamental.

C.explanation: A neutron is a hadron made of three quarks with composition $udd$, so it has internal structure.

D.explanation: A proton is a hadron made of three quarks with composition $uud$, so it has internal structure.
